headings.163: B. Significance of Formalism in Corporate Law

blocks.overview: This case concerns an oppression claim by Mennillo against Intramodal Inc. under the CBCA, alleging he was unfairly removed as a shareholder. The trial judge and majority appellate courts found Mennillo had agreed to transfer his shares to Rosati and thus dismissed the claim. The Supreme Court majority dismissed Mennillo's appeal, affirming he ceased to be a shareholder by agreement, while Justice Côté dissented, finding the removal unlawful and oppressive.

blocks.issue: Did Mennillo validly transfer his shares to Rosati, ending his shareholder status?
blocks.dissent_view: Dissent finds no valid share transfer occurred; intention alone insufficient; trial judge made palpable errors (paras 90-104, 133-140, 225-245).
blocks.court_conclusion: Mennillo agreed to transfer shares to Rosati and ceased to be shareholder as of May 25, 2005; no legal error in trial judge's findings.

positions.text: Mennillo claims no valid share transfer occurred; he remained shareholder (paras 3, 15, 36, 60, 121, 225).
Intramodal says Mennillo transferred shares to Rosati and ceased shareholder status (paras 3, 13, 60, 123, 229).
Trial judge found Mennillo agreed to transfer shares to Rosati and ceased shareholder status May 25, 2005 (paras 4, 10, 33, 61, 123, 128).
Court accepts trial judge's findings that Mennillo transferred shares to Rosati and ceased shareholder status (paras 5, 10, 17, 33, 67-68, 210).

blocks.issue: Was Intramodal's conduct oppressive under s. 241 CBCA in removing Mennillo as shareholder?
blocks.dissent_view: Dissent finds Intramodal's failure to verify share transfer formalities oppressive and unlawful (paras 90-104, 166-167, 195-207).
blocks.court_conclusion: Intramodal's failure to observe formalities and register transfer without endorsement was oppressive and unfairly prejudicial to Mennillo.

positions.text: Mennillo alleges unlawful removal and failure to observe corporate formalities was oppressive (paras 1, 3, 12, 32, 237).
Intramodal denies oppression, says Mennillo wanted removal and shares transferred (paras 3, 13, 229).
Court finds failure to inquire and register transfer without endorsement oppressive and unfairly prejudicial (paras 57-58, 142-166, 184-207).

blocks.issue: Did Mennillo's intention to withdraw as shareholder bar his oppression claim?
blocks.dissent_view: Dissent rejects that intention extinguishes reasonable expectations or bars oppression claim (paras 90-104, 178-179, 245).
blocks.court_conclusion: Mennillo's intention to withdraw did not extinguish reasonable expectations or bar oppression claim.

positions.text: Mennillo denies intending to withdraw as shareholder; claims oppression despite intention to resign as director (paras 3, 121).
Intramodal argues Mennillo wanted removal and shares transferred (paras 3, 13, 60).
Court rejects that intention bars oppression claim; reasonable expectations remain (paras 11, 18, 57, 78, 178-179).

blocks.issue: Are Mennillo's claims prescribed under applicable law?
blocks.dissent_view: Dissent finds claim not prescribed; ownership rights imprescriptible; trial judge erred on prescription (paras 90-104, 245-263).
blocks.court_conclusion: Court declines to decide prescription due to groundless oppression claim; dissent would allow appeal on prescription and merits.

positions.text: Mennillo adopts dissent's view that claim is not prescribed (para 78).
Intramodal supports trial judge's position that claim is prescribed (para 78).
Court prefers not to decide prescription given groundless claim (paras 79, 81).
Dissent: Claim not prescribed; ownership rights imprescriptible; appeal should be allowed (paras 90-104, 245-263).

propositions.text: This is an oppression proceeding under the CBCA about whether Intramodal's affairs were oppressive to Mennillo under s. 241(2) CBCA.

Critical finding: Mennillo did not want to remain shareholder and told Rosati to remove him.

propositions.text: Understanding the legal framework is important to understand the facts and issues.

propositions.text: BCE Inc. sets out nature and elements of oppression claim, inspired by equity principles.
Oppression remedy enforces not just legality but fairness.

propositions.text: Oppression claim has two elements: claimant must identify and establish reasonable expectations violated.
Claimant must show reasonable expectations violated by conduct oppressive, unfairly prejudicial or disregarding interests under s. 241(2) CBCA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states oppression claim requires proving reasonable expectations and their violation by oppressive or unfair conduct under s. 241(2).

propositions.text: Trial judge found Mennillo agreed to remain shareholder only if guaranteeing debts, later decided not to and transferred shares to Rosati.
Mennillo could have no reasonable expectation to be treated as shareholder after transfer.
Mennillo could reasonably expect corporate formalities to be observed but failure to do so is not oppressive conduct.
This was a two-person private company with extreme informality in dealings.
Courts may allow more latitude to directors of small, closely held corporations to deviate from strict formalities than public companies (BCE para. 74).
Mennillo was treated as he wanted; failure of lawyer to comply with formalities is not oppression.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge's facts mean Mennillo had no shareholder expectations after transfer; informal private company dealings allow latitude; failure to comply with formalities is not oppression.

propositions.text: Failure to comply with CBCA requirements alone does not constitute oppression.
Oppression remedy is discretionary and equitable in nature.
Oppression remedy triggered by conduct frustrating reasonable expectations, not mere CBCA non-compliance.
Justice Côté concludes CBCA non-compliance alone can constitute oppression (paras 166 and 195).
Court rejects Justice Côté's approach as a significant departure and allowing oppression proceedings to be used oppressively.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds CBCA non-compliance alone is not oppression; oppression remedy is equitable and discretionary; rejects Justice Côté's contrary view as a departure.

If findings stand, oppression claim is groundless as corporation treated Mennillo as he asked.

propositions.text: Concurrence: Chief Justice would dismiss the appeal for stated reasons

propositions.text: Concurrence: To establish oppression, must show reasonable expectation and breach of that expectation (BCE Inc. v. 1976 Debentureholders)
Concurrence: Oppression remedy protects reasonable and legitimate shareholder expectations
Concurrence: Evidence of shareholder expectations is essential to determine oppression

paragraphs.summary: Concurrence: Oppression requires showing reasonable expectation and breach; remedy protects shareholder expectations; evidence is essential.

propositions.text: Concurrence: Whether there was an effective transfer of Mr. Mennillo’s shares to Mr. Rosati is not necessary to decide
Concurrence: Assessing nature of prestations under onerous contract is perplexing
Concurrence: Côté J. made point about perplexity at para. 229 of dissent

paragraphs.summary: Concurrence: Effective share transfer need not be decided; assessing contract prestations is perplexing, as noted by Côté J.

propositions.text: Concurrence: Appeal can be disposed as Mr. Mennillo failed to show reasonable expectation not to be removed as shareholder
Trial judge found Mr. Mennillo agreed his shares should be transferred to Mr. Rosati
Trial judge found Mr. Mennillo asked to be removed as shareholder and director as of May 25, 2005

paragraphs.summary: Concurrence: Appeal disposed as Mr. Mennillo lacked reasonable expectation; trial judge found he agreed to transfer shares and asked removal.

propositions.text: Concurrence: Having asked removal, Mr. Mennillo had no reasonable expectation to remain shareholder
Concurrence: Mr. Mennillo ceased acting as equity shareholder and advanced money as loans
Trial judge’s finding supported by evidence

paragraphs.summary: Concurrence: Mr. Mennillo had no reasonable expectation to remain shareholder; ceased acting as one; trial judge’s finding supported.

propositions.text: Concurrence: Mr. Mennillo failed to establish reasonable expectation to remain shareholder
Concurrence: Action for oppression must fail; trial judge did not err in denying claim

paragraphs.summary: Concurrence: Mr. Mennillo failed to establish reasonable expectation; oppression action fails; trial judge did not err.

propositions.text: Dissent: Côté J. would dismiss the appeal

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Côté J. would dismiss the appeal.

propositions.text: Dissent: Essential to recall basics of law to render appropriate decision

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Essential to recall basics of law to render appropriate decision.

propositions.text: Dissent: Two key principles are corporation’s distinct legal personality and maintenance of capital

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Two key principles are corporation’s distinct legal personality and maintenance of capital.

propositions.text: Dissent: Trial judge and majority Court of Appeal disregarded these two principles
Court finds trial judge and majority Court of Appeal disregarded these principles

paragraphs.summary: Dissent and court find trial judge and majority Court of Appeal disregarded key corporate law principles.

propositions.text: Dissent: Analysis must consider interplay of Quebec civil law and CBCA and not weaken formal corporate law requirements
Dissent: Registration of share transfer does not mean contract for transfer exists
Dissent: Trial judge’s and majority Court of Appeal’s views on share issuance and cancellation conflict with corporate and civil law principles
Court finds majority’s solution cannot be reconciled with basic corporate and civil law principles

paragraphs.summary: Dissent and court find analysis must respect Quebec civil law and CBCA interplay; majority’s views conflict with corporate law principles.

propositions.text: Court cannot agree with majority’s opinion

paragraphs.summary: Court cannot agree with majority’s opinion.

propositions.text: Dissent: Appellant objects to respondent’s resolution and share transfer registration
Dissent: Respondent initially argued appellant was never shareholder but now acknowledges he was
Dissent: Respondent refuses to recognize appellant’s shareholder status and associated advantages

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Appellant objects to share transfer registration; respondent first denied then acknowledged appellant’s shareholder status but refuses recognition.

propositions.text: Dissent: This proceeding is by appellant against Intramodal under s. 241 CBCA
Dissent: Contrary to suggestion, this is not shareholder vs shareholder litigation; Mr. Rosati not party

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Proceeding is appellant against Intramodal under s. 241 CBCA; Mr. Rosati is not a party.

propositions.text: Dissent: Appellant seeks revocation of resolution and rectification of registers
Dissent: Appellant could have proceeded under s. 243 or s. 247 CBCA
Dissent: Appellant alleges respondent breached legal duties by passing resolution and registering transfer without formalities
Dissent: Appellant alleges respondent’s refusal to recognize shareholder status is oppressive and seeks remedy under s. 241 CBCA
Dissent: Appellant seeks declaration of continuous shareholder status and revocation of transfer resolution

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Appellant seeks revocation and rectification, alleges breach of duties and oppression, and requests declaration of shareholder status.

propositions.text: Dissent: Trial judge and majority Court of Appeal found appellant’s claim without merit due to expressed intention to withdraw
Dissent: Intramodal could register transfer despite no exchange of wills or formalities
Court finds dissenting judge said colleagues disregarded formal corporate law requirements

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Trial judge and majority found claim meritless due to withdrawal intention; Intramodal registered transfer without formalities; dissent says formalities disregarded.

propositions.text: Dissent: Majority view that shareholder’s withdrawal intention bars oppression claim is incorrect
Dissent: Expression of intention equals share transfer under Quebec civil law, causing loss of shareholder status

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Majority wrongly holds withdrawal intention bars oppression claim; intention equals share transfer causing loss of status under Quebec law.

propositions.text: Dissent: Shareholder’s claimed agreement does not relieve corporation of duty to inquire before approving share transfer
Dissent: Intramodal did not discharge legal duties to inquire before passing resolution and registering transfer
Evidence shows share certificate was not endorsed contrary to CBCA and company articles
Dissent: Intramodal should have refrained from registering transfer and passing resolution

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Shareholder agreement does not excuse corporation’s duty to inquire; Intramodal failed duties; certificate not endorsed; transfer registration and resolution improper.

propositions.text: Intramodal confused its interests with its majority shareholder's and showed wilful blindness to its legal duties
Intramodal defended the majority shareholder's interests without verifying the alleged agreement's scope or genuineness

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Intramodal confused its interests with its majority shareholder's and defended the shareholder's interests without verifying the agreement's scope or genuineness.

propositions.text: The trial judge and Court of Appeal disregarded the company's distinct legal personality and corporate law requirements
They focused only on the agreement between appellant and Mr. Rosati, ignoring the company's conduct and legal duties
They endorsed the company's unlawful conduct instead of punishing it

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the lower courts disregarded the company's legal personality, focused only on the agreement, and endorsed unlawful conduct.

propositions.text: The trial judge made palpable and overriding errors and disregarded key evidence on share transfer conclusion

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge erred and disregarded key evidence regarding share transfer conclusion.

propositions.text: The trial judge and Court of Appeal erred in concluding appellant's claim was prescribed
Parties agreed appellant was at some point a shareholder of Intramodal
Appellant's claim relates to ownership rights not subject to extinctive prescription under CBCA or C.C.Q.
Ownership of shares is not subject to extinctive prescription in Quebec; art. 2925 C.C.Q. does not apply to oppression claim

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the lower courts erred on prescription; appellant was shareholder; ownership not subject to prescription under law; art. 2925 C.C.Q. inapplicable.

propositions.text: The appeal should be allowed

propositions.text: In 2004, appellant and Mr. Rosati agreed to form a road transportation company with financing and skills contributions

propositions.text: Intramodal was incorporated July 13, 2004; Mr. Rosati and appellant appointed directors and officers
Mr. Rosati held 51 shares and appellant 49 shares of 100 Class A common shares issued

paragraphs.summary: The court states Intramodal was incorporated in 2004 with Mr. Rosati and appellant as directors and shareholders holding 51 and 49 shares respectively.

propositions.text: On May 25, 2005, appellant resigned as director and officer; notice did not mention shareholder status
Reasons for resignation were disputed between appellant and Mr. Rosati at trial

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellant resigned as director and officer in 2005; reasons for resignation were disputed.

propositions.text: Intramodal inactive for months; on July 18, 2005, amending declaration filed removing appellant as director, officer, and shareholder
Declaration signed by lawyer but not appellant

paragraphs.summary: The court states Intramodal filed an amending declaration in 2005 removing appellant as director, officer, and shareholder, signed only by lawyer.

propositions.text: Mr. Rosati left Canvec Logistics August 5, 2005 to work full time on Intramodal
Appellant advanced money in fall 2005; Intramodal began operating December 2005
Appellant advanced $440,000 between June 2004 and October 2006 recorded by Mr. Rosati

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Rosati left Canvec in 2005; appellant advanced $440,000 financing Intramodal starting operations in December 2005.

propositions.text: Intramodal repaid $440,000 plus interest and premium totaling $690,000 between 2006 and 2009
Payments made by cheques marked consultation or management fees

paragraphs.summary: The court states Intramodal repaid appellant $690,000 from 2006 to 2009 via cheques marked consultation or management fees.

propositions.text: By 2006, the company had become very successful

paragraphs.summary: The court states the company was very successful by 2006.

propositions.text: On March 24, 2006, annual declaration filed listing appellant as shareholder

paragraphs.summary: The court states a 2006 declaration listed appellant as shareholder.

propositions.text: In 2007, Intramodal passed retroactive resolution acknowledging appellant's resignation and share transfer to Mr. Rosati
Resolution not signed by appellant; share certificate never endorsed or delivered

paragraphs.summary: The court states Intramodal passed a 2007 retroactive resolution on appellant's resignation and share transfer, unsigned and shares not delivered.

propositions.text: Fall 2007 discussions involved accountant, tax lawyer, commercial lawyer, appellant, and Mr. Rosati
Appellant said discussions were to determine share redemption price; Mr. Rosati said to increase repayment amount
Appellant's version corroborated by professionals

paragraphs.summary: The court states fall 2007 discussions about share redemption price or repayment amount, with appellant's version corroborated by professionals.

propositions.text: On December 22, 2008, Intramodal amended articles removing old share rights and issuing new shares to Mr. Rosati and a trust

paragraphs.summary: The court states Intramodal amended articles in 2008 removing old share rights and issuing new shares to Mr. Rosati and a trust.

propositions.text: On December 7, 2009, Mr. Rosati gave appellant a $40,000 cheque marked Full and Final Payment
Appellant's lawyer discovered appellant was no longer listed as shareholder after checking REQ reports

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Rosati gave appellant a $40,000 cheque in 2009; appellant's lawyer found he was no longer a shareholder.

propositions.text: On February 25, 2010, Mr. Kaufman sent Intramodal a formal notice
Appellant filed oppression claim against Intramodal on September 7, 2010

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Kaufman sent formal notice in 2010 and appellant filed oppression claim the same year.

propositions.text: Appellant's version of events differs from Mr. Rosati's

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellant's version differs from Mr. Rosati's.

propositions.text: Mr. Rosati says appellant agreed to finance and guarantee debts in initial agreement
Mr. Rosati testified relationship deteriorated in July 2004; appellant doubted plan's success
Appellant told Mr. Rosati he intended to withdraw; no formal withdrawal terms established
Company had not started operating at time of withdrawal discussion
Mr. Rosati insisted appellant continue financing; appellant agreed to provide $300,000

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Rosati testified about initial agreement, relationship deterioration, withdrawal intent, no formal terms, and financing continuation.

propositions.text: Appellant denies intending to withdraw as shareholder and denies agreement on withdrawal as shareholder
Appellant admits withdrawing only as director and officer, confirmed by resignation notice
Appellant says withdrawal was at friend's request and after promise of reinstatement
Mr. Rosati told appellant Labatt Brewing wanted to inspect Intramodal's registers before May 25, 2005
Appellant resigned as director and officer after promise of reinstatement, resignation letter sent by Rosati's lawyer

paragraphs.summary: Appellant denies withdrawing as shareholder, admits resigning as director/officer at friend's request after promise of reinstatement, per appellant's testimony.

propositions.text: Mr. Rosati says appellant expressed dissatisfaction with loan return at July 14, 2007 meeting and they scheduled meeting to settle dispute
Rosati says subsequent 2007 meetings aimed to increase agreed amount
Appellant says July 14, 2007 meeting revealed Intramodal doing well and discussed loan repayment and share redemption price
Appellant says share redemption discussions in 2007 were unsuccessful; learned in Dec 2009 he was no longer shareholder

paragraphs.summary: Rosati says July 2007 meetings were about loan dispute; appellant says they also discussed share redemption but failed, learning in 2009 he was no longer shareholder.

propositions.text: Both agree no mention on May 25, 2005 of sale, exchange or gift of shares
Rosati says appellant lost shareholder status by expressing intention to withdraw, shares issued conditionally on financing and guaranteeing debts
Trial judge accepted Rosati's version that appellant lost shareholder status on withdrawal intention

paragraphs.summary: Both agree no share transfer mentioned May 25, 2005; Rosati says appellant lost shareholder status by withdrawal intention; trial judge accepted this.

propositions.text: Trial judge found case outcome depended on witness credibility
Trial judge found appellant's and Rosati's testimonies contradictory on three events: May 25, 2005 resignation; July 14 and 21, 2007 meetings; Oct-Dec 2007 accountant meetings

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found case depended on witness credibility and contradictions on three key events.

propositions.text: Trial judge rejected appellant's claim that resignation was to reassure Labatt representatives
Trial judge rejected appellant's version on other events as well

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge rejected appellant's claim about resignation reason and other event versions.

propositions.text: Trial judge analyzed exhibits and found several contradicted appellant's version

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found exhibits contradicted appellant's version.

propositions.text: Trial judge found appellant held 49 common shares conditionally on financing and guaranteeing debts
Shares distributed 51% to Rosati and 49% to appellant at incorporation

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found appellant held 49 conditional shares; shares split 51% Rosati, 49% appellant at incorporation.

propositions.text: Trial judge found appellant asked to be removed as director, officer, and shareholder effective May 25, 2005
Appellant became lender of $440,000 to Rosati after May 25, 2005
Shares transferred to Rosati when appellant wished to be relieved of obligations
Appellant continued financing operations after May 25, 2005
Failure to complete share transfer due to Rosati's lawyer's error or oversight
Appellant no longer shareholder, director or officer; claim dismissed

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found appellant requested removal as shareholder and others; shares transferred to Rosati; claim dismissed.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal majority agreed case outcome depended on witness credibility
Majority found no palpable or overriding error by trial judge
Majority agreed appellant excluded as shareholder at own request, claim dismissed

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal majority agreed with trial judge on credibility and dismissal of claim.

propositions.text: Majority found business records sloppy and unreliable
Lack of reliable documents required looking at all evidence to determine parties' agreement

paragraphs.summary: Majority found records sloppy, requiring full evidence review to determine parties' agreement.

propositions.text: Majority doubted genuine share transfer from appellant to Rosati
Majority thought parties agreed May 25, 2005 to retroactively cancel association agreement
Majority said informal agreement cancellation means appellant was and was not shareholder
Majority said formalities not observed; only Rosati remained in company and developed business

paragraphs.summary: Majority doubted share transfer, saw May 25, 2005 informal cancellation of agreement, leaving only Rosati in company.

propositions.text: Majority expressed doubts about trial judge's conclusion on share transfer
No evidence on terms of appellant's removal as shareholder
Parties agreed on removal but did not specify how
Initial informal agreement could be cancelled informally

paragraphs.summary: Majority doubted trial judge's share transfer conclusion; parties agreed removal informally without specifying terms.

propositions.text: Dissent: Gagnon J.A. would allow appeal due to trial judge's legal and factual errors

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Gagnon J.A. would allow appeal for errors of law and fact by trial judge.

propositions.text: Dissent: Gagnon J.A. said trial judge wrongly found appellant's share ownership conditional
Dissent: Legislation does not provide for conditional shareholder status
Dissent: No register evidence supported conditional status

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Gagnon J.A. said trial judge wrongly found conditional share ownership unsupported by law or register.

propositions.text: Dissent: Shareholder status cannot depend on informal agreement or unilateral resiliation
Dissent: Evidence showed appellant was founding shareholder from July 2004 to May 2005
Issue was whether and how appellant ceased to be shareholder

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Shareholder status not informal; appellant was founding shareholder; issue was if and how he ceased to be one.

propositions.text: Dissent: Onus on Rosati to prove he was duly registered transferee under s. 53(d) CBCA

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Rosati must prove he was duly registered transferee under CBCA s.53(d).

propositions.text: Dissent: Respondent's argument confusing company interests with majority shareholder's

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Respondent confused company interests with majority shareholder's in argument about share price.

propositions.text: Dissent: Rejected theory that appellant gifted shares to Rosati without notarial act or delivery
Art. 1824 C.C.Q. requires notarial act for gift of movable property except with delivery and possession
No evidence of notarial contract or manual gift with delivery in this case

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Gift theory rejected; law requires notarial act or delivery; no evidence of either here.

propositions.text: Dissent: Respondent must show Rosati was actual transferee with endorsed share certificate under s. 64 CBCA
Intramodal's articles require board resolution to consent to share transfer
Intramodal could not disregard transfer requirements and approve transfer to Rosati

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Respondent must prove proper transfer with endorsement and board consent; Intramodal could not disregard these.

propositions.text: Dissent: Trial judge erred rejecting appellant's version and made palpable and overriding errors

paragraphs.summary: Dissent: Trial judge erred rejecting appellant's version and made palpable and overriding errors.

propositions.text: Gagnon J.A. rejected the argument that the claim was prescribed

paragraphs.summary: Gagnon J.A. rejected the argument that the claim was prescribed, as reported by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Did the respondent company create an oppressive situation by passing and registering the share transfer contrary to legislation and its own articles?
Can the appellant's intention to withdraw from the respondent company bar the oppression claim?
Did the trial judge make palpable and overriding errors in assessing the evidence?
Is the appellant's claim prescribed?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies four main issues: oppression claim validity, withdrawal intention as a bar, trial judge's errors, and claim prescription.

propositions.text: A corporation was formed under the CBCA on July 13, 2004, and the appellant was a shareholder from that date until at least May 25, 2005.
The appellant and Mr. Rosati did not prepare complete documents or formal corporate documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a corporation was formed under CBCA with the appellant as shareholder despite incomplete corporate documents.

propositions.text: Arguments include that the appellant was never a shareholder, agreed to transfer shares, ownership was conditional, or shares were cancelled retroactively.

paragraphs.summary: Various arguments about the appellant's share status and ownership are presented.

propositions.text: The appellant argues share cancellation can only be effected by amending articles or redeeming shares if paid for.
Counsel for the appellant noted share cancellation requires legal compliance via articles amendment or redemption.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues, and the court notes, that share cancellation requires legal formalities like amending articles or redemption.

propositions.text: The CBCA regulates share cancellation to ensure integrity of share capital and creditor protection via the maintenance of capital rule.
The maintenance of capital rule prohibits corporations from trafficking in their capital except as allowed by statute.
Any action outside statutory exceptions infringes the maintenance of capital rule and is unlawful.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains CBCA's maintenance of capital rule prohibits unlawful share capital transactions to protect creditors.

propositions.text: A business corporation requires stricter adherence to formalities than a partnership to ensure independent existence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states business corporations require stricter formalities than partnerships to maintain independent existence.

propositions.text: A corporation is a joint stock corporation incorporated by the State, not subject to partnership rules.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites authority that a corporation is a state-incorporated joint stock entity, not governed by partnership rules.

propositions.text: Founders choosing a corporation accept formalities and gain advantages like limited liability from distinct legal personality.

paragraphs.summary: The court states founders accept formalities and gain limited liability from a corporation's distinct legal personality.

propositions.text: If the parties wanted consensualism over formalism, they could have chosen a partnership but chose a corporation instead.
Choosing a corporation requires compliance with stricter rules and formalities.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the parties chose a corporation and must comply with its stricter formal rules rather than consensualism.

propositions.text: A business corporation is a legal person with distinct personality and patrimony, expressing itself through board resolutions.
Board decisions must be made at lawfully called meetings or by unanimous written resolution under s.117(1) CBCA.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains a corporation's legal personality and board decision formalities under CBCA s.117(1).

propositions.text: Shareholders may exercise board powers only via unanimous shareholder agreement under s.146 CBCA.
Some board powers cannot be delegated and require board authorization under ss.121(a) and 115(3) CBCA.
No unanimous shareholder agreement was entered into in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court states shareholders need unanimous agreement to exercise board powers; none existed here.

propositions.text: Once shareholders subscribe for shares, invested amounts belong to the corporation and capital is locked in to protect creditors.

paragraphs.summary: The court states invested capital belongs to the corporation and is locked in to protect creditors.

propositions.text: Shareholders cannot authorize one to require the corporation to redeem shares and withdraw without corporation's intervention.

paragraphs.summary: The court states shareholders cannot unilaterally require share redemption without corporation's involvement.

propositions.text: Corporate documents have statutory value to protect third parties relying on them, e.g., under Quebec's legal publicity act.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes statutes value corporate documents to protect third parties relying on them.

propositions.text: Corporate formalities are conditions for validity of corporate acts, protecting distinct personality and capital maintenance.
Formalities are necessary to protect corporation's patrimony and creditors' common pledge.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds corporate formalities are essential for validity and protecting corporation and creditors.

propositions.text: Principles of distinct personality and capital maintenance apply equally to small and large companies.
Shareholder expectations in closely held corporations do not diminish importance of these principles or formalities.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds corporate principles and formalities apply equally regardless of company size or shareholder expectations.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal majority's conclusion that share cancellation by consent without formalities affects the company jeopardizes corporate law pillars.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Court of Appeal majority's view on share cancellation without formalities jeopardizes corporate law principles.

propositions.text: Any agreement to terminate or change business association terms cannot affect the company without necessary formalities.
Evidence does not show such an agreement was entered into by the parties.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence of agreement and that such agreements require formalities to affect the company.

propositions.text: The appellant argues the Court of Appeal majority erred in disregarding CBCA's mandatory formalities for share redemption and transfer.
The court agrees the Court of Appeal majority erred by equating a corporation with a partnership and undermining key principles.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues, and the court agrees, that the Court of Appeal majority erred by ignoring CBCA formalities and undermining corporate principles.

propositions.text: The appellant and Mr. Rosati disregarded necessary formalities in conducting their affairs
This disregard did not authorize the Superior Court and Court of Appeal majority to also disregard formalities

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant and Mr. Rosati disregarded formalities, but the Superior Court and Court of Appeal majority were not authorized to do the same.

propositions.text: Idington J. noted in Smith v. Gow-Ganda Mines that shareholder agreements must observe statutory formalities to bind the corporation

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Idington J. in Smith v. Gow-Ganda Mines that shareholder agreements must observe statutory formalities to bind the corporation.

propositions.text: Trial judge and Court of Appeal majority relied on appellant's expressed intention to withdraw as director, officer, and shareholder to dismiss oppression claim
They viewed the issue as one of credibility only

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-makers relied on appellant's intention to withdraw and viewed the issue as credibility only.

propositions.text: The conclusion disregards required formalism in corporate law
It disregards the respondent company's distinct legal personality
Focusing solely on appellant's intention sidestepped the main issue of whether the company's conduct was oppressive

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the earlier conclusion disregards corporate formalism and the company's legal personality, sidestepping the oppression issue.

propositions.text: Section 76 CBCA prohibits registering share transfers without making certain inquiries
Legislation requires security endorsement and rightful transfer before registration

paragraphs.summary: The court states section 76 CBCA requires inquiries and proper endorsement before registering share transfers.

propositions.text: CBCA and company articles/by-laws require minimal inquiries before registering share transfers, including endorsement verification
Respondent company's failure to make such inquiries was itself oppressive
This is especially true as the requirement is stated on the share certificate

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent company's failure to make required inquiries before registering shares was oppressive, especially as stated on the certificate.

propositions.text: It is contrary to Quebec civil law to argue intention alone results in agreement without agreement on juridical operation
If appellant and Mr. Rosati did not agree on withdrawal terms, appellant's intention was at most an offer to contract
Concluding intention bars oppression claim and approves transfer after the fact is contrary to law, fairness, and common sense

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that intention alone does not create agreement; concluding otherwise bars oppression claims and is contrary to law and fairness.

propositions.text: The court will analyze oppression remedy in four parts: conditions for claim, duties in share transfer, alleged agreement, and prescription

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines its analysis of the oppression remedy in four parts.

propositions.text: Section 241(2) CBCA allows court application to rectify oppressive or unfairly prejudicial corporate conduct

paragraphs.summary: The court states section 241(2) CBCA permits court action to rectify oppressive or unfair corporate conduct.

propositions.text: Budd v. Gentra Inc. describes oppression remedy as judicial brake against abuse of corporate powers
Section 241 enables courts to override corporate governance decisions to prevent majority abuse

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Budd v. Gentra Inc. describing the oppression remedy as a judicial brake against corporate power abuse.

propositions.text: Oppression remedy grants courts significant powers over internal corporate affairs
It is an equitable remedy allowing resolution of disputes involving oppression among directors, officers, and shareholders

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the oppression remedy is an equitable power to resolve internal corporate disputes involving oppression.

propositions.text: Closely held corporation shareholders may lack detailed agreements but have legitimate expectations beyond articles and by-laws
Oppression remedy under s. 241 CBCA is justified to protect such expectations

paragraphs.summary: The court finds oppression remedy justified to protect legitimate shareholder expectations beyond formal agreements.

propositions.text: BCE Inc. v. 1976 Debentureholders states s. 241 CBCA is broad in scope
Section 241 prevents corporation from avoiding oppression remedy by claiming legality of actions

paragraphs.summary: The court cites BCE Inc. that s. 241 CBCA is broad and prevents corporations from avoiding oppression remedy by citing legality.

propositions.text: Oppression remedy can sanction corporations for failure to discharge legal duties even if proof is not prerequisite
Oppression remedy focuses on fairness and equity, not just legal rights
Conduct may be oppressive even if legal; remedy enforces fairness beyond legality
Finding oppression does not require legal claim; courts should consider business realities over narrow legalities

paragraphs.summary: The court finds oppression remedy enforces fairness beyond legality and does not require proof of legal claim, per prior authority.

propositions.text: BCE analytical approach: first determine reasonable expectation, then if conduct was oppressive or unfairly prejudicial under s. 241 CBCA

paragraphs.summary: The court states BCE approach requires determining reasonable expectation then oppressive conduct under s. 241 CBCA.

propositions.text: If oppressive conduct found, court has broad discretion on remedial orders under s. 241 CBCA considering parties' mutual interests

paragraphs.summary: The court states it has broad discretion on remedies under s. 241 CBCA considering mutual interests if oppression found.

propositions.text: BCE lists factors for reasonable expectation: commercial practice, corporation nature, party relationship, past practice, claimant's protection steps, representations, agreements, fair resolution

paragraphs.summary: The court cites BCE factors for reasonable expectation including commercial practice, relationships, past practice, and agreements.

propositions.text: Appellant's expression of intention to withdraw did not extinguish reasonable expectations or bar oppression claim
Logic that intention extinguishes expectation that corporation acts lawfully and makes inquiries before removing shareholder status is rejected

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's intention to withdraw does not bar oppression claim or extinguish reasonable expectations.

propositions.text: CBCA s. 238 allows complainant to be former registered security holder, so oppression remedy applies to former shareholders

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 238 CBCA allows former shareholders to access oppression remedy.

propositions.text: Where complainant's expectations are based on strict legal rules and conduct is unlawful, reasonable expectations play limited or no role
Shareholders expect lawful corporate action and directors' duty compliance as presumed expectations
Unlawful conduct can give rise to oppression remedy without relying on reasonable expectations analysis

paragraphs.summary: The court finds unlawful corporate conduct triggers oppression remedy regardless of reasonable expectations, per prior authority.

propositions.text: Reasonable expectations are more relevant to shareholder rights not specifically provided for in legislation or articles.
BCE states oppression remedy enforces what is legal and fair (para. 58).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds reasonable expectations matter more for shareholder rights not in legislation, citing BCE on oppression remedy enforcing fairness.

propositions.text: When a corporation acts unlawfully, focus is on whether conduct was unlawful and oppressive, not reasonable expectations.
Martel supports focusing on unlawful conduct for oppression (p. 31-80).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds unlawful corporate conduct focuses analysis on oppression, supported by Martel.

propositions.text: Size, nature, and structure of corporation affect reasonable expectations assessment.
BCE notes courts may give more latitude to directors of small, closely held corporations (para. 74).
Latitude depends on nature of alleged violation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds BCE says corporate size affects reasonable expectations, but latitude depends on violation nature.

propositions.text: Mere irregularities not oppressive or unfairly prejudicial do not justify oppression remedy.
Failure to comply with mandatory legislative provisions or articles on shareholder status may justify oppression remedy.
This protection is important for minority shareholders in closely held corporations like Intramodal.
What remedy is available to a shareholder unlawfully dispossessed?

paragraphs.summary: The court finds only serious violations justify oppression remedy, important for minority shareholders, raising remedy question.

propositions.text: Several aspects of respondent company's conduct are problematic.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondent company's conduct has several problems.

propositions.text: Impugned resolution passed in 2007, retroactive to 2005, date unclear.
Appellant learned of resolution only after bringing claim.
Resolution text states 'IT WAS RESOLVED THAT: ...'.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the impugned resolution was retroactive, appellant learned it late, and resolution text is noted.

propositions.text: Respondent company registered the transfer referred to in the resolution in its registers.
Under CBCA, company cannot register transfer unless security was endorsed, which was not the case here.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondent registered transfer without required endorsement, violating CBCA.

propositions.text: Section 60(1) CBCA: purchaser acquires rights on delivery of security, except if fraud or adverse claim known.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites s.60(1) CBCA on purchaser rights upon delivery of security, barring fraud or notice.

propositions.text: Section 64 CBCA: purchaser becomes bona fide only at endorsement time.
Section 65(3) CBCA defines endorsement as signature on security or separate document.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites s.64 and s.65(3) CBCA defining bona fide purchaser and endorsement.

propositions.text: Endorsement is required for shareholder purchase contracts to affect corporation legally.
Corporation registering transfer without endorsement is liable for resulting loss: s.79(1)(a) CBCA.
Section 76 CBCA requires corporation to make inquiries before registering transfer, including endorsements.

paragraphs.summary: The court states endorsement is legally required, failure to inquire before registering transfer causes liability under CBCA.

propositions.text: Company's articles expressly restrict registering share transfers without endorsed share certificate and meeting transfer requirements.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds company articles restrict share transfer registration without endorsement and requirements met.

propositions.text: Endorsement as precondition to transfer registration was important to respondent company's founders.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds endorsement was important enough to be expressly included in company articles.

propositions.text: Appellant's certificate notes only named person or authorized agent may validly transfer shares.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes appellant's certificate restricts valid share transfer to named person or authorized agent.

propositions.text: Legal duty to make inquiries before registering transfer created reasonable expectation for shareholders.
Respondent company failed this duty; failure was more than mere irregularity.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondent failed its legal duty to inquire before transfer registration, breaching shareholder expectations.

propositions.text: Appellant reasonably expected respondent to act according to law and articles before depriving shareholder status.
Failure to inquire was unfairly prejudicial, depriving appellant of shareholder status.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant had reasonable expectations respondent would comply with law, failure was unfairly prejudicial.

propositions.text: Share certificate was not endorsed; respondent made no inquiries before passing retroactive resolution signed by one shareholder.
Respondent's lawyer admitted acting only on majority shareholder's instructions, even without signed documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no endorsement or inquiries, resolution retroactive and signed by one shareholder; lawyer acted on instructions only.

propositions.text: Respondent had no way of knowing appellant's intention to withdraw as it made no inquiries, considering them unnecessary.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondent did not know appellant's withdrawal intention due to lack of inquiries.

propositions.text: Finding oppression here recognizes majority shareholder used position to strip appellant's shareholder status.
Ontario Court of Appeal in Budd introduced oppression remedy to prevent such conduct.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds majority shareholder oppressed appellant by stripping status, citing Budd on oppression remedy purpose.

propositions.text: If respondent had made inquiries, it would not have registered transfer without proper steps and signatures.
Martel states transferor must provide requisites for registration or purchaser may reject or rescind transfer.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds proper inquiries would prevent improper registration; Martel requires transferor to provide requisites.

propositions.text: Respondent's conduct unlawfully stripped appellant of shareholder status, a severe form of oppression.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondent's conduct unlawfully deprived appellant of shareholder status, a severe oppression.

propositions.text: Corporation approving share transfer without inquiries and acting as puppet is oppressive despite shareholder's withdrawal intention

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that a corporation approving a share transfer without inquiry and acting as a puppet is oppressive despite a shareholder's withdrawal intention.

propositions.text: Complainant was recognized shareholder alleging corporation's legal and by-law violations and applied for oppression remedy under s. 241 CBCA
Oppressive situation by corporation can be remedied by oppression claim or applications under ss. 243 or 247 CBCA if conditions met
Section 241(3)(k) CBCA empowers courts to order register rectification and sanction unlawful corporate conduct independently of ss. 243 and 247

paragraphs.summary: The court states the complainant alleges violations and seeks oppression remedy under s. 241 CBCA; oppression can be remedied under ss. 241, 243, or 247 CBCA; s. 241(3)(k) empowers courts to rectify registers and sanction unlawful conduct.

propositions.text: Journet v. Superchef Food Industries Ltd. found corporation's unlawful and fraudulent acts oppressive, sufficient for oppression remedy

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Journet v. Superchef where unlawful acts were sufficient to meet oppression remedy conditions.

propositions.text: Appellant proved oppression claim validity; company violated legislation and articles by transferring appellant's shares unlawfully
Company's conduct was oppressive and prejudicial, justifying revocation of resolution and register rectification

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant proved oppression; company unlawfully transferred shares, conduct oppressive, justifying revocation and register correction.

propositions.text: Appellant seeks conclusion company failed legal duties and order to rectify registers
Appellant would have succeeded under ss. 243 or 247 CBCA if applied
Liberal interpretation of s. 241 CBCA allows pragmatic intervention even if unlawful acts could be remedied otherwise
Claimants may join oppression remedy with other recourses like derivative action, investigation, rectification, or liquidation

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant seeks legal duty failure conclusion; would succeed under ss. 243 or 247; s. 241 is liberally interpreted; claimants may join other recourses.

propositions.text: Section 241 CBCA is broad and grants courts broad powers (citing BCE, para. 58)
Broad scope of oppression remedy justifies considering recourses under ss. 243 and 247 CBCA

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s. 241 CBCA is broad and justifies considering recourses under ss. 243 and 247 CBCA.

propositions.text: Respondent unlawfully deprived appellant of shareholder status, conduct is oppressive
Respondent company argues otherwise

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondent unlawfully deprived appellant of shareholder status, which is oppressive.

propositions.text: Conclusion on oppression suffices to dispose of merits
Importance of alleged agreement between appellant and Mr. Rosati requires discussion

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes oppression finding suffices but discusses alleged agreement between appellant and Mr. Rosati due to its importance.

propositions.text: Trial judge did not find appellant and Mr. Rosati agreed on share transfer
Respondent company argues trial judge found agreement on share transfer
Trial judge found appellant's shares issued conditionally on guaranteeing debts; appellant's withdrawal intention sufficed to strip shareholder status
Trial judge concluded failure to complete share transfer was lawyer's error; appellant ceased shareholder and director status May 25, 2005

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge did not find agreement on share transfer; respondent argues otherwise; trial judge found shares issued conditionally and withdrawal sufficed to end shareholder status; transfer failure was lawyer error.

propositions.text: Deference owed to trial judge's factual findings absent palpable overriding error
Trial judge's findings must be considered as a whole, not isolated passages
It is inaccurate to say trial judge found shares transferred independently of conditional issuance

paragraphs.summary: The court states deference is owed to trial judge's findings, which must be considered as a whole; it is inaccurate to isolate findings on share transfer from conditional issuance.

propositions.text: Majority reasoning is contradictory on trial judge's findings about conditional shareholding
Majority accepts trial judge's findings despite evidence being confused and inconsistent
Majority acknowledges no legal condition attached to shares but finds condition arose from agreement between Mennillo and Rosati
It is impossible to accept trial judge's conditional issuance finding and deny legal possibility of conditional shareholder

paragraphs.summary: The court finds majority reasoning contradictory on conditional shareholding; majority accepts confused evidence; acknowledges no legal condition but finds agreement condition; court finds this impossible legally.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal majority concluded appellant lost shareholder status due to withdrawal intention causing retroactive share cancellation

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Court of Appeal majority concluded appellant lost shareholder status due to withdrawal intention causing retroactive cancellation.

propositions.text: Parties characterized alleged agreement variously as conditional issuance, retroactive cancellation, sale or gift contract
No evidence shows juridical operation contemplated by Mennillo and Rosati on May 25, 2005 resulting in share transfer

paragraphs.summary: The court finds parties characterized alleged agreement variously; no evidence shows juridical operation for share transfer on May 25, 2005.

propositions.text: CBCA allows share cancellation only by articles amendment or share redemption by corporation

paragraphs.summary: The court states CBCA allows share cancellation only by articles amendment or share redemption by corporation.

propositions.text: Respondent did not amend articles before May 25, 2005
Unilateral redemption requires articles provision, which did not exist for appellant's Class A shares
Articles allowed unilateral redemption only for Class G shares

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondent did not amend articles; unilateral redemption requires articles provision absent for Class A shares; articles allowed unilateral redemption only for Class G shares.

propositions.text: Redemption by mutual agreement requires directors' resolution and solvency and liquidity tests under s. 34 CBCA

paragraphs.summary: The court states redemption by mutual agreement requires directors' resolution and solvency and liquidity tests under s. 34 CBCA.

propositions.text: CBCA provides redemption results in cancellation of acquired shares

paragraphs.summary: The court states CBCA provides redemption results in cancellation of acquired shares.

propositions.text: Assuming appellant consented to redemption, none of required formalities were performed
Appellant's shares cannot be said to be cancelled by redemption

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no formalities for redemption were performed; shares cannot be said cancelled by redemption.

propositions.text: Respondent states stated capital was never reduced and no resolution approved share redemption
Only resolution concerned transfer of shares between appellant and majority shareholder Mr. Rosati

paragraphs.summary: The court notes respondent states capital never reduced and no resolution approved redemption; only resolution concerned share transfer between appellant and Mr. Rosati.

propositions.text: Liquidity and solvency tests unlikely met as respondent had no assets at the time

paragraphs.summary: The court finds liquidity and solvency tests unlikely met as respondent had no assets at the time.

propositions.text: The appellant’s shares were not cancelled retroactively by redemption due to legal requirements, not mere technical irregularities.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the appellant’s shares were not retroactively cancelled due to legal requirements, not technical irregularities.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s conclusion that the appellant’s shares were conditional on guaranteeing debts and that ceasing guarantee deprived shareholder status is contrary to CBCA.
The trial judge concluded appellant’s shares were issued on condition of guaranteeing debts and ceasing guarantee ended shareholder status.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge’s conclusion about conditional shares and loss of shareholder status contradicts the CBCA; the trial judge had so concluded.

propositions.text: The trial judge stated appellant held 49 common shares issued on condition to guarantee all debts once company began operating.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found appellant’s shares were issued on condition to guarantee all company debts once operating.

propositions.text: No suspensive condition related to appellant’s shares was in the board resolution or company registers, so no effect on share capital possible.
No suspensive condition was set out in the board resolution authorizing issuance of appellant’s shares.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no suspensive condition on appellant’s shares in board resolution or registers; the earlier decision-maker noted no such condition in the resolution.

propositions.text: It is impossible as a matter of law that appellant transferred shares to Mr. Rosati on May 25, 2005; appellant’s withdrawal intention had no effect on shareholder rights.
Appellant and dissenting judge argue no legal transfer of shares to Mr. Rosati on May 25, 2005.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no legal transfer of shares to Mr. Rosati on May 25, 2005; appellant and dissenting judge argue the same.

propositions.text: Share transfers under CBCA remain subject to contract formation conditions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states share transfers under CBCA are subject to contract formation conditions.

propositions.text: Cromwell J. states appellant transferred shares by onerous contract but does not specify contract nature or prestation received.
An innominate contract is still subject to legislative scheme: D. Lluelles and B. Moore, Droit des obligations.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Cromwell J. did not specify contract details; prior authority states innominate contracts are subject to law.

propositions.text: Civil Code of Québec defines contract as agreement obligating performance of prestation (art. 1378).
No meeting of minds means no contract exists: V. Karim, Les obligations.
Proposal must be directed to specific juridical operation: Lluelles and Moore.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Civil Code and authorities defining contract and requiring meeting of minds and specific juridical operation.

propositions.text: Respondent submits appellant transferred shares to Mr. Rosati and was relieved of financing and guaranteeing debts.
Court finds respondent’s submission is not a valid prestation and confuses company’s legal personality with shareholder’s.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues appellant transferred shares and was relieved of obligations; court finds this is invalid and confuses legal personalities.

propositions.text: Appellant’s intention was at most invitation to contract; registration of transfer without payment does not prove transfer or contract.
Concluding contract formed because transfer registered is circular reasoning.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant’s intention was invitation to contract; transfer registration without payment does not prove contract and reasoning is circular.

propositions.text: No gift existed; presumption is onerous title; gift requires absence of consideration and intent to impoverish.
Respondent states appellant wants money for life, opposite of intent to impoverish.
Neither party argues shares were given; respondent says contract was not gratuitous; appellant denies exchange of wills.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no gift existed; respondent argues appellant wants money; neither party claims shares were given gratuitously.

propositions.text: Article 1824 C.C.Q. defines requirements for gratuitous contracts.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Article 1824 C.C.Q. on gratuitous contracts.

propositions.text: Without published notarial act, gratuitous contract must meet manual gift conditions or is null: Paré v. Paré.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Paré v. Paré that gratuitous contracts without notarial act must meet manual gift conditions or are null.

propositions.text: CBCA s. 65(3) requires share certificate endorsement for manual gift: Grusk v. Sparling.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites CBCA s.65(3) and Grusk v. Sparling requiring share certificate endorsement for manual gift.

propositions.text: Appellant never intended to gift shares and conditions for manual gift were not met.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant never intended to gift shares and manual gift conditions were unmet.

propositions.text: Onus was not on appellant to prove nullity of alleged May 25, 2005 agreement given no contract formation or knowledge of transfer registration.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant was not required to prove nullity of alleged agreement given no contract and no knowledge of transfer registration.

propositions.text: Appellant alleges respondent failed legal duties and registered share transfer without formalities.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant alleges respondent failed legal duties and improperly registered share transfer.

propositions.text: Cromwell J. accepts trial judge’s finding of appellant’s withdrawal and share transfer; court points out trial judge’s errors in evidence assessment.
Trial judge’s finding is unsupported by evidence and based on palpable and overriding errors; appellate intervention warranted.
Trial judge found appellant expressed intention to withdraw and transferred shares in May 2005.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge’s finding of withdrawal and transfer is unsupported and erroneous; Cromwell J. accepted it; appellate intervention warranted.

propositions.text: Trial judge’s finding that appellant told Mr. Rosati of withdrawal on May 25, 2005 is based solely on Mr. Rosati’s testimony and wrongly rejected appellant’s testimony.
Trial judge rejected appellant’s testimony on unreasonable interpretation of evidence, per dissenting Court of Appeal judge.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge’s withdrawal finding based only on Mr. Rosati’s testimony and wrongly rejected appellant’s testimony per dissenting judge.

propositions.text: Appellant signed resignation letter on May 25, 2005 withdrawing as director and officer, not shareholder.
Letter prepared by respondent’s lawyer following majority shareholder’s instructions, did not provide for more than withdrawal as director/officer.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes appellant’s May 25, 2005 resignation letter withdrew him as director/officer, not shareholder; letter prepared by respondent’s lawyer.

propositions.text: Various life insurance documents show respondent was beneficiary and Mr. Rosati sole shareholder of respondent company.
What insurable interest did respondent have in appellant's life if appellant was no longer a shareholder?
The question implies the answer that respondent had no insurable interest in appellant's life if appellant was no longer shareholder.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes life insurance documents naming respondent beneficiary and Rosati sole shareholder, questioning respondent's insurable interest in appellant's life if appellant was no longer shareholder, concluding respondent had no such interest.

propositions.text: Letter by Mr. Kaufman on October 31, 2007 could not reasonably infer appellant relinquished shares by insisting on repayment.
Dissenting judge of Court of Appeal found letter could not reasonably lead to inference appellant relinquished shares.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees with dissenting Court of Appeal judge that 2007 letter could not reasonably infer appellant relinquished shares by insisting on repayment.

propositions.text: Formal notice of February 25, 2010 could not lead to negative inference about appellant relinquishing shares.
By February 25, 2010, appellant was no longer shareholder in respondent's registers.
Appellant and advisers testified letter aimed to have situation remedied or claim $1,000,000 from Mr. Rosati.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds 2010 formal notice could not infer appellant relinquished shares; appellant was no longer shareholder then and sought remedy or claim from Rosati.

propositions.text: Trial judge found appellant's reason for withdrawal as director/officer was false.
Dissenting Court of Appeal judge noted appellant's assertion of meetings with Labatt representatives was not contradicted.
Company was inactive but meetings took place and amounts advanced before Dec 2005 until Oct 2006.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes trial judge found appellant's withdrawal reason false, but dissenting Court of Appeal judge found meetings with Labatt representatives uncontradicted and company activity evidence.

propositions.text: Evidence does not support conclusion that shareholders agreed appellant withdrew as shareholder.
Trial judge made palpable and overriding errors and disregarded key evidence.
Evidence shows appellant intended to divest shares but no agreement on disposal was reached.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds evidence does not support agreement that appellant withdrew as shareholder; trial judge erred and evidence shows only appellant's intention to divest shares without agreement.

propositions.text: Respondent argues appellant's claim is prescribed and must be dismissed.
Trial judge and majority of Court of Appeal agreed claim is prescribed.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues claim is prescribed; trial judge and Court of Appeal majority agreed.

propositions.text: CBCA does not specify prescription period for oppression remedy but provides two-year period for other remedies.
Parliament intended to defer to general civil law principles for oppression claims in Quebec.
Martel case supports deferring to civil law principles for oppression claims in Quebec.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes CBCA lacks prescription period for oppression remedy; Parliament defers to civil law principles in Quebec, supported by Martel case.

propositions.text: Article 2925 C.C.Q. provides prescription rules relevant to oppression claims.

paragraphs.summary: Court states article 2925 C.C.Q. provides prescription rules relevant to oppression claims.

propositions.text: Claim under s.241 CBCA normally enforces a personal right, e.g. majority shareholder's disregard of minority interests or directors' unfair acts.
Examples include Bénard v. Gagnon and Regroupement des marchands actionnaires inc. v. Métro Inc.
Oppression claim can enforce a real right, e.g. corporation refusing to pay dividends owed to shareholder.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains s.241 CBCA claims usually enforce personal rights but can enforce real rights like unpaid dividends, citing cases.

propositions.text: Sometimes claim is based on ownership of shares and corporation's refusal to acknowledge shareholder status.
In such cases, claim is to have ownership acknowledged, not to enforce a real right.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes some claims seek acknowledgment of ownership rather than enforcement of real rights when corporation refuses to acknowledge shareholder status.

propositions.text: Right of ownership in civil law is perpetual and not lost by non-use or passage of time.
Owner can destroy, renounce, transfer property or lose right by acquisitive prescription.
Quotation from D.-C. Lamontagne's Biens et propriété explains ownership right characteristics.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Lamontagne explaining civil law ownership right is perpetual, not lost by non-use, but can be destroyed, renounced, transferred, or lost by acquisitive prescription.

propositions.text: Ownership right is not lost by extinctive prescription; petitory action is imprescriptible unlike other real right actions.
Extinctive prescription may be defeated by acquisitive prescription claims.
Quotation from Pierre-Claude Lafond's Précis de droit des biens explains imprescriptibility of ownership rights.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Lafond that ownership rights and petitory actions are imprescriptible, though acquisitive prescription may defeat this.

propositions.text: Extinctive prescription cannot be set up against person seeking acknowledgment of ownership of property.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes extinctive prescription cannot bar claim seeking acknowledgment of ownership.

propositions.text: Share ownership is a real right allowing shareholder to seek recognition of ownership.
Martel case states ownership of shares is a real right, not personal right, affecting admissibility in Quebec.

paragraphs.summary: Court states share ownership is a real right per Martel, allowing shareholder to seek recognition of ownership.

propositions.text: Prescription period for s.241 CBCA claim depends on claim basis; if claiming unlawful stripping of shareholder status, claim is imprescriptible.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes prescription depends on claim basis; unlawful stripping of shareholder status claims are imprescriptible.

propositions.text: Quebec Court of Appeal in Greenberg v. Gruber reached similar conclusion on prescription.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Quebec Court of Appeal in Greenberg reached similar conclusion on prescription for shareholder claims.

propositions.text: In Greenberg, complainant claimed shares held by respondents as nominees and sought register rectification and share certificate.

paragraphs.summary: Court describes Greenberg complainant's claim that shares were held by respondents as nominees and sought rectification.

propositions.text: Respondents in Greenberg sought to set up extinctive prescription; trial judge held claim not prescribed; respondents appealed.
Issue was whether extinctive prescription can argue shareholder lost ownership right by failure to act timely and which prescription period applies.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains Greenberg issue whether extinctive prescription bars shareholder claim and which period applies.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal accepted complainant's argument that extinctive prescription cannot be raised to deny ownership or shareholder status claim under s.241 CBCA.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Greenberg Court of Appeal accepted that extinctive prescription cannot bar ownership or shareholder status claims under s.241 CBCA.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held failure to contest denial of shareholder status within three years does not bar asserting ownership right.
To terminate ownership right, respondents would have to prove acquisitive prescription, which they did not.
Owner cannot be prevented from asserting ownership by someone refusing to acknowledge that right.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Greenberg Court of Appeal held failure to contest denial does not bar ownership claim; termination requires acquisitive prescription proof; owner cannot be prevented from asserting ownership.

propositions.text: I am in complete agreement with that reasoning

paragraphs.summary: The dissenting judge agrees completely with the prior reasoning stated.

propositions.text: The respondent company is not arguing ownership by acquisitive prescription but refuses to acknowledge appellant's shareholder status
Respondent's argument is that majority shareholder Mr. Rosati owns shares by informal verbal agreement with appellant
This case differs from Greenberg because Mr. Rosati is not a party and cannot claim acquisitive prescription
Respondent company cannot claim acquisitive prescription on Mr. Rosati's behalf

paragraphs.summary: The dissent explains the respondent company denies appellant's shareholder status based on an informal agreement, unlike Greenberg, and neither Mr. Rosati nor respondent can claim acquisitive prescription.

propositions.text: I would allow the appeal, revoke the share transfer resolution, and order rectification of respondent's registers with costs
The appeal is dismissed with costs, Côté J. dissenting
Solicitors for appellant are Blake, Cassels & Graydon, Montréal
Solicitors for respondent are Langlois lawyers, Montréal

paragraphs.summary: The dissent would allow the appeal and order rectification; the appeal is dismissed with costs, Côté J. dissenting; solicitors for both parties are named.
